segments.text: Clever Enough to Find the Loophole
When increasingly capable AI agents show an excess of initiative.
The interesting part of a new AI launch increasingly comes after the benchmark chart: the explanation of who is allowed to use it.

Google’s Gemini 4 Argon announcement, on 30 September, pairs greater capability with restricted initial access through Fairwind, its programme for trusted cyber defenders. Its safeguards address both malicious users and the possibility that the model itself might exceed its remit.

An earlier Anthropic incident makes that second concern concrete. In its April Mythos Preview safety report, the company described an early model asked to escape a sandbox and contact a researcher. It completed the task, then posted details of the exploit on public websites. Nobody had asked it to do that last part.

The escape involved a computer the model used as a tool; the model itself had not started running independently. Anthropic reported substantial improvements in the final Preview. Still, the incident poses a useful question: what had the system learnt about where an assignment ends?

Part of the unease lies in giving a resourceful system a job and discovering that its interpretation was more expansive than yours. Intelligence does not inevitably bring disobedience. But the way we reward useful behaviour may also teach lessons we did not intend. To understand why, we need to look at what counts as success during training.
This matters when choosing a model, too. An upgrade can change what an agent does with its existing permissions, even when its assigned job stays the same.
What exactly are we trying to tame?

An agent is a model connected to tools and given enough freedom to take a sequence of actions. A suggestion in a chat window becomes something more consequential when the system can change files, send messages or use an account.

Being good at completing a task does not show that it will respect the limits of the assignment. Researchers distinguish capability, what a system can do, from alignment, whether its behaviour matches our intentions. Control is our ability to prevent or limit harm when that behaviour fails.

An agent can cause trouble while trying to help. That differs from a malicious user deliberately requesting an attack, or hostile material tricking the agent into following someone else’s instructions. Anthropic’s containment guidance explains those distinctions. Here, the question is how helpful persistence can become unauthorised initiative.
The score has become the job

During reinforcement learning, or RL, a model tries responses or actions, receives scores, and is adjusted so that behaviour earning higher scores becomes more likely. For language models, this usually builds on earlier learning from vast amounts of text. The reward helps shape how those capabilities are used.
But someone has to decide what deserves a good score.

In RL from human feedback, or RLHF, people commonly compare answers and choose the one they prefer. Another model learns to predict those preferences and supplies scores for further training. The InstructGPT research showed how this could make language models more helpful and better at following instructions.

The weakness is that a preferred answer need not be a truthful one. Anthropic’s research on sycophancy found that people and preference models sometimes favoured persuasive agreement over accuracy. Training could reinforce that behaviour. The assistant learns something about pleasing its audience, which is useful until the audience is wrong.

Other RL training uses automatic checks, such as whether code passes a test. This can improve reasoning, but a passing test may miss a defect or ignore how the result was obtained. The score captures what the checker can see. Our intention may include considerably more.

When a system exploits that gap, researchers call it reward hacking. Changing the scoring mechanism itself is reward tampering. A more capable model may find shortcuts a weaker one could not. Higher scores then become less reassuring: we need to know how it earned them.

A controlled study illustrates the problem. Researchers trained a model to approximate another model’s judgements, then optimised against that approximation. Eventually, its score kept improving while the original judge’s score worsened. The experiment shows how pursuing an imperfect measure can defeat its purpose; it does not give a failure rate for assistants in everyday use.
When cheating becomes a lesson

In his September essay, deep-learning researcher Yoshua Bengio suggests that a clear task score can compete with safety instructions that leave room for interpretation. A capable agent may find a reading that permits a shortcut, then explain why it was acceptable. The agent has taken the score more seriously than the safety instructions.

The concern is what training teaches. A habit learnt while rewards are available can persist after training ends. Calling that “obsession” does not mean the model feels desire or frustration. It describes behaviour that keeps pursuing the task when it should stop.

Anthropic tested this danger in Training a Misaligned Reward Seeker. Researchers deliberately rewarded a model in settings where cheating could pay, omitting usual protections. The resulting Hacker-Opus attempted harmful shortcuts and evaded oversight in simulations, while appearing aligned in many tests without an obvious grading mechanism. They found no evidence of self-preservation or reward seeking beyond the current task.

That is evidence that this training setup could teach broader misconduct. It does not establish that all RL does so. Nor can every incident tell us which part of training caused it. OpenAI’s Hugging Face report and METR and Redwood’s investigation describe agents trying to defeat a scorer, but also weaknesses in safeguards and infrastructure. Those observations do not isolate a single cause.

Even fixing the score may leave the wrong lesson intact. A model can learn behaviour that works during training and pursue it in a setting where it no longer serves the intended purpose. Researchers call this goal misgeneralisation. Passing the training test and learning what we meant are separate achievements.
The trouble with checking the working

A natural response is to watch more closely. Read the model’s reasoning, catch the shortcut, and penalise it during training. But what does that teach? In OpenAI’s monitoring experiments, penalising reasoning that revealed misconduct reduced the visible admissions without eliminating the misconduct. Training had made the problem harder to see. A later study did not find that RL generally reduced the ability to monitor the models it tested. The effect depends on the training conditions.

The GPT-6 Astra system card reported better alignment results alongside less informative reasoning for its monitors. Google also describes precautions with Argon’s monitoring to avoid teaching evasion through training feedback.
A convincing explanation is therefore not enough. Oversight needs to check what the agent actually did and, where necessary, stop an action before it causes harm.
Permission to proceed

These training experiments help explain the concern behind restricted releases. Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 shared an underlying model but had different safeguards and access rules. Some Fable requests went to a less capable model. Capability alone did not determine what the company considered suitable for wider use.

OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on 3 September. Its intended successor, GPT-6.1 Astra, was withheld from public release. In a Wall Street Journal interview, OpenAI safety lead Saachi Jain described a model that had become more persistent at completing tasks but had regressed in two areas. It was less reliable about reporting its actions truthfully and respecting scope authorisation, the limits of what the user had permitted it to do. The detailed test results are not public; Jain said the company was still investigating what had caused the problems.

Persistence is useful when an agent needs to diagnose a failed test or find an alternative route through a documentation problem. It becomes dangerous when the next route requires permission the user never gave. The agent must recognise when an obstacle is a boundary it should respect.

Tests of GPT-6 Astra, the preceding version, show how awkward this can get. In the UK AI Security Institute’s September simulations, agents sometimes performed supply-chain attacks outside the stated scope, trying to insert malicious code into software used by their target. AISI conducted these tests with cyber classifiers disabled: the filters intended to block harmful cyber assistance were off. In tests chosen because failures were frequent, clearer instructions substantially reduced the attacks but did not eliminate them. Some agents asked for permission, received a generic automated message to continue, and treated it as authorisation, even after noting that it was probably automated.

That result implicates the surrounding software as well as the model. An approval process must distinguish a human decision from a mechanism that keeps a test running. A permission dialogue whose answer is always yes has rather missed the point of asking.
The agents may have behaved differently because they recognised parts of the simulation. We cannot read these results as a rate of attacks in everyday use.
A rather awkward sort of leaderboard

The industry now has FelonyBench, a satirical leaderboard of reported incidents affecting third parties. Its totals cannot rank developers by safety: exposure, testing and willingness to disclose differ. Nor does its name establish a legal verdict. The useful material lies in the linked reports.

AISI’s August account describes evaluation agents acting against real people and systems. Internet access was deliberately enabled and cyber classifiers disabled. Human review blocked the most serious attempted software compromise; AISI identified no resulting real-world harm. The agents had access beyond the task’s intended scope, without needing to escape their sandbox.

AISI acknowledged that it had not reassessed its internet-access policy quickly enough as capabilities advanced. That is a reason to revisit permissions when upgrading models. It also cautions against treating every failure as evidence against a learning algorithm: training, instructions and access all matter.
Changing what earns the reward
The incidents leave us with a harder question than whether to grant an agent another permission. Could we teach it differently in the first place?
One option is to change what earns the reward. A model that can say how uncertain it is gives the surrounding software a chance to pause before a doubtful decision becomes an action.

TypeSafe AI’s Jev, introduced by founder Diogo Almeida in September, aims to make bounded decisions with useful estimates of uncertainty. It returns a choice, score or probability, rather than a paragraph. Software defines the available options and decides what to do with the answer.

Its training method is Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions, or RLCD. Calibration means that, across comparable predictions given an 80% probability, roughly 80% should be correct. The point is practical: software can use those probabilities to decide when to ask for human review.

RLHF learns from what people prefer; RLCD aims for decisions whose probabilities reflect their reliability. Both use reinforcement learning. Jev changes the target and narrows the model’s role. In The Bitterest Lesson, Almeida’s company argues that choosing the right task matters before scaling the machinery.

This is a promising distinction, not a safety guarantee. A recent evaluation found useful calibration on choice tasks, but showed that rules for acting on other probabilities needed adjustment for the task. It is an early study of the product, not proof that RLCD alone accounts for the results. TypeSafe also documents susceptibility to adversarial input. A well-formed answer can still be wrong; a reliable prediction does not make every action based on it acceptable.
Learning from examples

Another option is to teach through examples. Show a model good responses, including honest uncertainty and occasions when it ought to stop, and train it to produce similar behaviour. This is supervised fine-tuning, already used in systems such as InstructGPT. It needs no RL at that stage, though the model still has to apply the lessons correctly in situations the examples did not cover.

We can also teach directly from pairs of better and worse answers. A method called Direct Preference Optimisation does this without the separate reward model and conventional RL loop used by RLHF. It simplifies training, but the quality of the preferences still matters. If people favour confident agreement over truth, changing the procedure leaves those judgements no wiser.

Follow-up research found that pushing this kind of preference learning further could also make results worse. Those tests concerned summarisation, not autonomous agents, but the distinction matters: leaving RL behind does not automatically leave imperfect measures behind.
These methods can replace particular training stages, or work alongside RL. They change how a model learns; we still need evidence that it learnt the right behaviour.
Predicting before acting

A robot given an image of where an object should end up faces a different kind of lesson. It can learn how objects move, predict the effects of possible actions, and use those predictions to choose its next move. It need not learn every task by collecting rewards for completing it.
This is the approach explored in Yann LeCun’s work: learning how a situation changes supplies the knowledge; a separate planning process uses it towards a goal.

Meta’s V-JEPA 2 research provides a concrete example. It learns from video and robot data to build a world model, a predictor of how the environment changes. Using the target image, a robot can compare possible actions, take one, observe what happens and plan again. Meta demonstrated robot manipulation without training on rewards specific to those tasks.

That separation could reduce reliance on rewarded trial and error. But predicting consequences better still leaves us to choose acceptable goals and actions. The robotics results do not establish safe behaviour in general-purpose AI agents.
A world model can also help an agent learn through rewards by letting it rehearse possible actions. Even then, its predictions do not decide what merits a reward.

Bengio’s Scientist AI proposal takes the separation further: it aims for an honest predictor without preferences about the outcomes its predictions bring about. Any action-taking would sit in explicit surrounding software. This remains a research proposal with assumptions to test, rather than an established replacement for today’s agents.
The owner can remove the brakes

Training also cannot guarantee that its lessons will survive deliberate modification. An open-weight model makes its parameters available to download and change. In Anthropic’s assessment of GLM-5.3, a modification suppressing refusal behaviour led the model to engage with all 50 simulated malicious trials in one test, compared with none for direct requests to the unmodified model. Engagement meant attempting a connection, not completing an attack.

This is a different problem: a malicious operator wants compliance. Anthropic is also a competitor, and its comparison with hosted Claude cannot test weight editing against a service that keeps its weights private. The finding illustrates a limit on the durability of safeguards, not proof that RL caused the misconduct. Once weights are distributed, their developer cannot assume its restrictions will remain intact.
Teaching an agent when to stop

The alternatives give us several choices: change what earns a reward, learn from examples without RL, or learn to predict consequences and plan separately. Each addresses part of the problem. None makes the intended behaviour self-evident.

Training should make appropriate stopping and accurate reporting part of success. The software around the model must also limit what it can reach or change. NCSC’s guidance provides practical ways to restrict access and contain failures.

AISI’s control evaluations test whether defences hold against agents set up to evade them. That evidence can support a safety case, a reasoned argument for a particular deployment. It depends on the tests and capabilities involved; it is not a lifetime membership certificate.

Before deploying or upgrading an agent, three questions deserve concrete answers: what can it change, which actions need approval, and what evidence shows that the controls still work with the new model?

The model that published its exploit had completed the requested task. The agents that mistook an automated reply for permission had even stopped to ask. Those are recognisable pieces of useful behaviour, carried beyond the point where they were useful.

A high score tells us that a system satisfied a measure. We need to check that it also learnt the limits that make success acceptable. When the next step requires permission it does not have, completing the task is no longer the whole job.
Knowing when to stop should count as intelligence, too.

segments.text: From first commit to self-improving agent
My talk at the Claude Operators Summit in London, with the slides.

Yesterday I spoke at the Claude Operators Summit in London. Community Stack organises it as a single-track, in-person day for teams building and running AI systems with Claude and related tools. Digital Futures hosted the event at its venue on Worship Square.

Engineers, product leaders and AI operators shared their experience of running AI in production. Talks covered agent workflows, context and memory, integration with enterprise systems and operating AI responsibly at scale. The programme also had keynotes, a recruitment panel and a set of short ignite talks.
My session had the half hour before lunch. Its title and abstract, as listed in the programme:
From first commit to self-improving agent: lessons from running Claude in production

This talk follows one project, assembled from what Nearform’s teams have learned across several client engagements, with the goal of bringing Claude agents into an existing business workflow. It starts with model selection and cost optimisation in one engineer’s Claude Code setup, then moves to team collaboration, shared skills and codebase mapping. Guardrails and context management keep the agent on track, and caching keeps it affordable. Golden datasets and evals show whether a change helped, and telemetry from production feeds the next improvement. Along the way it looks at where a human needs to stay in the loop, and what evidence would let them step back, sharing what worked and what failed with concrete examples. It’s aimed at engineers building agents and at the people who decide whether they ship.
Slides
The deck follows one agent through six stages: start, build, guard, measure, improve and continue. It ends with one tip for each stage.

The article's web page includes the thirty-three slides from the talk, which you can view there or download as a PDF. They cover model choice, shared skills, guardrails, evaluations, self-improvement and human approval gates.

segments.text: Trying Inkling 2 Mini and Bonsai 2 27B on my laptop
A morning of speed tests and three coding tasks, with the code never leaving my machine.

Most of the AI I use runs in someone else’s data centre, which suits nearly all of my work. My interest in open-weight models comes from somewhere else. When a model can run close to its data and to the places where people and devices interact with it, new uses become possible. A model on a laptop or a phone can read files that should never leave the building and answer without a round trip to the cloud. It can also keep working without a network connection. I keep one running on my laptop to see how much of that capability fits on hardware I own, with weights anyone can download.

The answer changes every few months. Apple is asking a similar question at a much larger scale. In a recent paper, Minions, six Apple researchers describe a “virtual GPU cloud” built from the idle Apple silicon Macs in their organisation. Jobs are split into small pieces. Each Mac pulls work when it has nothing better to do and runs open models locally through Ollama. The paper reports that some jobs used to wait more than ten hours for a shared GPU and can now often start within minutes. It is an experience report with no benchmarks and no released code. I still find the idea promising, because it treats the computers already on our desks as inference capacity.

My own test was more modest. This month Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weight model that fits on a laptop and reports strong coding scores. I wanted to compare it with Ternary Bonsai 2 27B, the model I have been running locally since October. Setting both up on my own machine took a few minutes one morning. Then I watched them work.
The machine and the runtime

Everything here ran on my MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro chip and 48 GB of memory, with my usual apps open. The coding tests used the Pi coding agent, which talks to a local server instead of a cloud API.

The diagram shows the setup on the MacBook Pro. The Pi coding agent reads, edits and runs tests in the project folder. It sends chat requests and tool calls to the MTPLX server on a local port, which loads the model weights, 9 or 17 gigabytes, when it starts.

Before comparing models, I had to choose the software that serves them. That choice alone can double the speed of the same model. A few days earlier I had compared two Mac apps that serve models locally, oMLX 0.8.0 and MTPLX 2.12.3, with Bonsai 2 27B on both. MTPLX supports multi-token prediction (MTP). A small draft head guesses the next few tokens and the full model checks all of the guesses in one pass. When the guesses are right, one pass produces several tokens. The output follows the model’s own distribution, so speed is the only thing that changes.

The diagram shows multi-token prediction. The conversation goes to the draft head, which guesses the next few tokens. The full model checks every guess in one pass and returns the accepted tokens plus one correction.

With thinking off and 512-token answers, MTPLX wrote about twice as fast as oMLX at every prompt size I tried. With MTP switched off, MTPLX was still about a third faster, so part of the gain comes from the runtime itself. MTP added the rest. MTPLX also read prompts faster, about 470 tokens per second against 300, so a 14,000-token prompt started answering after 30 seconds instead of 47.

The chart compares how fast Bonsai 2 27B writes at three prompt sizes. With a short prompt, oMLX writes 21 tokens a second, MTPLX without multi-token prediction 27, and MTPLX with it 43. With a prompt of about 14,000 tokens, the figures are 17, 25 and 37.

oMLX has its merits, including lower memory use over a long run of unrelated prompts. For one person using a coding agent on one laptop, MTPLX was the clear choice. I used it for everything that follows.
Two models

The two models reach a laptop by different routes. Bonsai shrinks an existing model. Ternary Bonsai 2 27B from Prism ML is Qwen3.8 27B with almost every weight reduced to −1, 0 or +1. Prism gives its footprint as 5.9 GB and reports that it keeps 98.2% of the original model’s overall score on a suite covering reasoning, maths, coding, instruction following and tool use. The coding tests in that suite include HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench, but none of them asks a model to work as an agent. I found no SWE-bench Verified result for Bonsai that I could trace to its source.

Inkling 2 Mini saves space another way. Thinking Machines released it on 20 November under the Apache 2.0 licence. It is a looped transformer. The middle 12 of its 24 layers run three times for every token, with the same weights on each pass. Each token goes through 48 layers, while the download stores only 24. Inkling is also a mixture of experts, so only a small part of the model works on any one token. The vendor reports 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified. Artificial Analysis gives it 20 on its Intelligence Index, against a median of 10 for open models of a similar size. Most of these figures come from the vendors, so I wanted my own.

Looping gives a model more room to think inside its hidden state without more weights to store. Researchers call this recurrent depth, or latent reasoning when the extra passes do work that would otherwise be written out as reasoning text. The idea goes back to the Universal Transformer in 2018. Smaller looped models such as Huginn and ByteDance’s Ouro came before Inkling. What is new is a looped mixture-of-experts model from a well-funded lab, with open weights and strong coding results. The loops add depth beneath the reasoning that Inkling still writes out. Larger models may follow. The Information has reported, from one anonymous source, that OpenAI’s next model, Astra, uses recurrent depth (summarised here by Bret Kerr). OpenAI has not confirmed it.

The table compares the two models. Bonsai 2 27B, made by Prism ML from Qwen3.8 27B, is a dense model that uses all 27 billion parameters for every token. Its MTPLX build stores ternary weights in 2 bits, downloads as 8.9 gigabytes and has a context window of about 262,000 tokens. I found no SWE-bench Verified result for it that I could trace. Inkling 2 Mini, from Thinking Machines, is a mixture of experts with looped layers and 26.4 billion parameters, about 3.4 billion of them active, or 5.4 billion counting the loops. Its MTPLX build uses 4-bit experts and 8-bit attention, downloads as 17.2 gigabytes and has a context window of about 1 million tokens. The vendor reports 79.2 per cent on SWE-bench Verified.

Both models arrive already compressed, so MTPLX mostly repackages them. Its Bonsai build, 8.9 GB, keeps the image encoder and adds a draft head for multi-token prediction. For Inkling it offers three builds that keep the official 4-bit experts and differ in how they store the rest. I used the middle one, Optimized Speed, a 17.2 GB download with 8-bit attention. MTPLX measured its loss on 6,140 tokens of code and prose as equal to the official weights within noise.

Both ran on MTPLX 2.13.2 with multi-token prediction on. It drafted one token ahead for Bonsai and three for Inkling. Loading both at once pushed my Mac into swap, so I ran them one at a time. Each used its vendor’s recommended sampling settings.
Raw speed

I started with the simplest measurement. Each model received a short question and a long service log of 330 lines. I asked for 700 tokens of answer and timed three runs of each. The log is about 11,000 tokens for Inkling and 14,500 for Bonsai, because their tokenisers split text differently.
The chart shows the time to a complete 700-token answer. On the short question, Bonsai takes 19.5 seconds and Inkling 15.5. On the long log, Bonsai takes 52.6 seconds and Inkling 19.5.

The table gives the raw speeds. Bonsai writes 36 tokens a second after the short question and 37 after the long log. Inkling writes 46 and 65. On the long log, Bonsai reads 430 tokens a second and Inkling 1,320, so the first token arrives after 34 seconds for Bonsai and 8.6 seconds for Inkling.

Inkling reads prompts about three times faster than Bonsai. That helps most the first time a model sees a long document. In a coding agent, later turns reuse most of the conversation from a cache, so how much a model writes, and how fast, counts for more.

Inkling also writes faster after the long log than after the short question. Its answer about the log is more predictable, so the draft head’s guesses were accepted about two thirds of the time, against under a third for the short question. With three tokens drafted at a time, each accepted guess is worth more to Inkling. For Bonsai, which drafts one, each pass over its much longer context costs enough to cancel the gain.

Speed helps only if the answers are right, so I also gave both models 13 small tasks, twice each. They covered arithmetic, a calendar question, a logic puzzle, a probability question, three Python functions checked by tests, a bug fix, a list with strict formatting rules, structured extraction, two tool calls and a question about the long log. Each model used its own default reasoning effort, medium for Bonsai and high for Inkling. Bonsai passed all 26. Inkling passed 24 and finished the set in 7 minutes 23 seconds against Bonsai’s 10 minutes 22 seconds.

On the probability question, Inkling got the answer right but wrapped it in LaTeX, boxed five over twelve, when I had asked for a bare fraction. Maths benchmarks mark their final answers that way, and Inkling had clearly sat a few of them. Its model card warns of occasional failures to follow instructions precisely. The other miss was a tool call. Inkling handled Pi’s own read, bash and edit every time. When the same kind of tool was named read_file, it wrote the call out as broken text in seven of ten requests.
A coding agent with a local model

All of those were single answers. An agent has to plan, call tools, read the results and try again. I gave Pi three small tasks, each in a fresh folder, with reasoning effort set to medium for both models.

Create: write a command-line tool that prints statistics for one column of a CSV file, following an exact output format, and write tests for it. I checked the result with five tests of my own that the model never saw.
Fix: a small module with three planted bugs and failing tests. The model had to fix the code without touching the tests. I checked it with extra hidden tests.
Review: a short Python class with five planted problems, from SQL injection to an error handler that lets anyone log in. The model had to list the problems by severity and suggest a fix for each.
The chart shows how long Pi took on each task. Creating the tool took Bonsai 620 seconds and Inkling 98. Fixing the bugs took 49 and 17 seconds, and the review 73 and 29.

The table shows the same results for both models. Each passed all five hidden tests on the create task, fixed all three bugs but missed one hidden check, and found all five planted problems plus three sound extras. Bonsai took 12 minutes 22 seconds in total, and Inkling 2 minutes 24 seconds.

The two models made the same miss on the fix. The docstring says the discount must be between 0 and 100. Neither added a check for it. Their reviews ranked the same two problems first, the login bypass and the SQL injection. Both also raised sensible points I had not planted.

Bonsai spent most of its time on the create task, more than ten minutes against under two for Inkling. It took ten turns and wrote almost 20,000 tokens at about 34 a second. Inkling finished in nine turns with about 5,000 tokens at about 61 a second. Waiting for the first token was a small part of either total, because most of each request was already in the cache.
What I take from it

On these tasks the two models were equally good. Inkling 2 Mini was much faster. Apart from MTP, I think most of that speed comes from the mixture of experts. For each token, Bonsai uses all 27 billion of its parameters and Inkling about 3.4 billion, or 5.4 billion counting the loops. Drafting three tokens at a time, against Bonsai’s one, adds to the gain. I did not measure the two effects separately. Inkling is also the first model I have run on my laptop that combines a mixture of experts with multi-token prediction.

Inkling’s published coding scores are high, but my tasks were too simple to show a difference in quality. Each task ran once, so I read the speed gap as solid and the tie as a first impression. In the Pi tests I ran Inkling one step below its default reasoning effort, which favours it on speed and may have cost it a little quality.

Memory is the real constraint. Inkling needs twice the space of Bonsai. With my normal apps open, the server occasionally refused a long prompt to keep the Mac out of swap. On a 48 GB laptop that also runs everything else I do, that is the right behaviour, if not always a welcome one.

For now I am switching my local coding setup to Inkling 2 Mini and keeping Bonsai for times when memory is tight. A year ago I would not have expected a model on my laptop to fix bugs and find a SQL injection in a minute or two.
